content: To improve early childhood development, nurturing care must be provided. This includes promoting health, ensuring proper nutrition, maintaining safety and security, offering responsive caregiving, and creating opportunities for early learning. Parents and caregivers should be supported in delivering this nurturing care framework. The World Health Organization (WHO) child growth standards emphasize the importance of growth monitoring combined with growth promotion activities, such as nutrition counseling. Focusing on growth promotion and intensive nutrition counseling during all child health contacts is more effective than growth monitoring alone. Breastfeeding and complementary feeding counseling are critical components of child health. However, studies indicate missed opportunities to provide these services during immunization visits. For example, in Bangladesh, while 88% of children under two years received immunizations, only 8% of mothers reported receiving breastfeeding or complementary feeding information during these visits. Health workers should use counseling techniques to reinforce priority messages, such as the benefits of breast milk for physical and brain development and its protective effects against illness. Immunization visits can be used to gather information about breastfeeding practices and provide brief counseling, but time constraints often limit the feasibility of more extensive support. In Italy, immunization visits were used to assess breastfeeding rates, revealing lower rates than national and global recommendations. Similarly, in Tasmania, Australia, a study evaluated the feasibility of collecting infant feeding data during vaccination visits. While these visits allowed brief discussions on infant feeding, they were not well-suited for comprehensive breastfeeding support due to the already busy nature of immunization consultations. Dedicated primary health consultations for infant feeding may be more effective. Vitamin A supplementation is essential for children aged 6–59 months to support rapid growth and combat infections. Deficiency in vitamin A can lead to visual impairment and increased risk of illness and death from infections like measles and diarrhea. Vitamin A can be safely provided in large doses, stored by the body, and released over time. It is also crucial during pregnancy for visual health, immune function, and fetal development. Many countries have successfully integrated vitamin A supplementation into routine immunization services and campaigns, such as child health weeks. For example, in Sierra Leone, mass vitamin A supplementation every six months during mother and child health weeks reached over 85% of children aged 6–59 months. Integration with routine immunization, nutrition, and family planning services further increased coverage. A revised child health card was developed to include routine vitamin A supplementation at six months, deworming, and updated growth charts, along with information on breastfeeding, complementary feeding, and hygiene. Operational challenges with vitamin A supplementation include the need to cut capsules and administer them correctly, as well as different doses for different age groups. Careful documentation and integration with other nutrition interventions, such as micronutrient powders and nutritional counseling, should be considered. Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) are another critical intervention, particularly in malaria-endemic regions. Continuous distribution of LLINs through antenatal and child immunization services is a key strategy to protect vulnerable groups, such as pregnant women and young children. Countries should aim for universal coverage, defined as one LLIN for every two people at risk of malaria, using a combination of mass campaigns and continuous distribution through multiple channels.
